issues: The note says the Act was 'Passed by Parliament on 19 March 2022'. That is wrong. Parliament passed the bill, with amendments, on 9 March 2022 (Ada Derana, 9 March 2022: 'Personal Data Protection Bill was passed in parliament today (March 09) with amendments.'). The date 19 March 2022 is when the Speaker certified it, and the Act itself is headed '[Certified on 19th of March, 2022]'. The DLA Piper quote (and the DPA's own Background page) repeat this confusion. The DLA quote also misnames the law as 'the Personal Data Act No. 9 of 2022'.

The note calls it 'the first dedicated data-protection law in South Asia' as a plain fact. That is the Data Protection Authority's own claim. It is defensible, because Nepal's Individual Privacy Act 2018 came earlier but is a general privacy statute, and India's Act followed in 2023. Still, the claim should be attributed to the DPA.
'Amended by Act No. 22 of 2025' is correct. The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act, No. 22 of 2025 was certified on 30 October 2025 and gazetted on 31 October 2025.

The note leaves out that most of the Act is not yet in operation. DLA Piper (2026) says only the regulator and interpretation provisions have been brought into force, and the substantive Parts wait for a ministerial order that has not yet been made.

fieldFixes.note: Passed by Parliament on 9 March 2022 and certified by the Speaker on 19 March 2022. The Data Protection Authority calls it the first law of its kind in South Asia. Amended by the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act, No. 22 of 2025. So far only the provisions setting up the Data Protection Authority (and the definitions) are in operation; the substantive obligations await a ministerial commencement order.

issues: The note says 'Commencement is by notification'. That is out of date as of September 2026. MeitY notified the DPDP Rules, 2025 in November 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E) is dated 13 November 2025 and was gazetted on 14 November; PIB reports 14 November). The Act commences in phases. The provisions setting up the Data Protection Board took effect on 13 November 2025, the consent-manager provisions take effect on 13 November 2026, and the other substantive obligations take effect on 13 May 2027. Until then the IT Act 2000 and the 2011 Rules continue to govern (DLA Piper).

All other claims check out. The gazette header reads 'THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (NO. 22 OF 2023) [11th August, 2023.]', and the Act received presidential assent on 11 August 2023. The Puttaswamy judgment was in 2017. The earlier regime was the IT Act 2000 and the 2011 SPDI Rules (DLA Piper). The Data Protection Board of India is the regulator under s.18.

fieldFixes.note: Received presidential assent on 11 August 2023, after the Supreme Court's 2017 Puttaswamy judgment; before it, India relied on the IT Act 2000 and its 2011 rules. The Act commences in phases under the DPDP Rules, 2025, notified in November 2025. The provisions setting up the Data Protection Board of India took effect on 13 November 2025, and most substantive obligations take effect on 13 May 2027. Until then the IT Act regime continues to apply.

issues: The note says the ordinance's status after the elected parliament returned 'was not verified'. It has since been settled. On Thursday 9 April 2026 Parliament passed the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2026 as one of 31 bills dealing with interim-government ordinances (UNB/Financial Express). The official Laws of Bangladesh site lists the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 as Act No. 63 of 2026, dated 10 April 2026. Section 44(1) of that Act repeals Ordinance No. 61 of 2025 and the amending Ordinance No. 23 of 2026. Under s.1(3) the Act is deemed in force from 6 November 2025, except s.23 and ss.31–35, which start on a date the government gazettes once 18 months have passed. The Laws of Bangladesh page for the ordinance says it 'has been repealed by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 (Act No. 63 of 2026)'.

The record gives no ordinance number or exact date. The official listing gives Ordinance No. 61 of 2025, dated 6 November 2025. This matches the Prothom Alo report that the notifications were issued 'on Thursday' (6 November 2025).
The record also leaves out the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 (Ordinance No. 23 of 2026). Digital Policy Alert dates it to 5 February 2026.
The Prothom Alo source's date field reads '2025-11'. The page metadata gives datePublished 2025-11-09.

fieldFixes.law: Personal Data Protection Ordinance, 2025 (Ordinance No. 61 of 2025); replaced by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 (Act No. 63 of 2026)
fieldFixes.note: Promulgated by the interim government as Ordinance No. 61 of 2025, dated 6 November 2025, alongside a National Data Governance Ordinance, and amended in February 2026. After the elected parliament returned, it passed the Personal Data Protection Bill on 9 April 2026. The resulting Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 (Act No. 63 of 2026, dated 10 April 2026) repealed the ordinances and is deemed in force from 6 November 2025, except for a few sections (s.23 and ss.31–35) that take effect later by gazette notification.

issues: The note says the Act applies to private-sector entities 'with annual turnover of at least AUD 3 million'. That wording comes from DLA Piper and is slightly wrong. Small business operators with turnover of $3 million or less are exempt, so coverage starts above $3 million. The OAIC says 'organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, and some other organisations'. The note also leaves out the smaller organisations that are covered anyway, such as health service providers.

'The private sector was added by later amendment' is vague. The OAIC says the Privacy Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 extended coverage to some private-sector organisations from 21 December 2001. The OAIC also says the Act was passed at the end of 1988 and commenced in 1989.
The Act number (No. 119, 1988), the original coverage of Commonwealth agencies, and the OAIC as regulator all check out.

fieldFixes.note: Enacted as Act No. 119 of 1988 (commenced 1989) for Commonwealth agencies. The Privacy Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 extended it to private-sector organisations from 21 December 2001. It now covers most Australian Government agencies, organisations with annual turnover of more than AUD 3 million, and some smaller organisations.

issues: No errors found. The PCPD 'Key Facts and History' page gives 'The Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO) was enacted on 3 August 1995' and, in its 1996 row, 'The PDPO came into force on 20 December 1996'. yearEnacted 1995, inForce 1996, the Cap. 486 title and the PCPD as regulator all match. The existing quote covers only the enactment date, so the in-force sentence from the same page is added as a second source.

'One of Asia's earliest comprehensive laws' has no source and is hedged. It is reasonable: Japan's 1988 act and Taiwan's 1995 act covered only computer-processed data or the public sector. A small caveat not worth a field change: s.33 of the PDPO, on cross-border transfers, has never been brought into force, so 'in force 20 December 1996' holds for the Ordinance generally, as the PCPD says.
